<h1 id="Paper-014-%E2%80%94-Directed-Evolution-via-Selection-Algorithms">Paper 014 — Directed Evolution via Selection Algorithms<a class="anchor-link" href="#Paper-014-%E2%80%94-Directed-Evolution-via-Selection-Algorithms">¶</a></h1><p><strong>Dolson, E., Banzhaf, W., &amp; Ofria, C. (2022).</strong> Artificial selection methods from evolutionary computing show promise for directed evolution of microbes. <em>eLife</em>, <em>11</em>, e79665. <a href="https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.79665">https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.79665</a></p>
<p><strong>Summary.</strong> Compares 5 selection algorithms (random, truncation, tournament, lexicase, down-sampled lexicase) on multi-objective fitness. Lexicase preserves diversity better while maintaining fitness compared with truncation-style aggregate pressure—a pattern consistent with the computational evidence in Dolson et al.</p>

<li>Adapted from <code>control/directed_evolution/directed_evolution.py</code></li>

<div class="cell border-box-sizing text_cell rendered"><div class="inner_cell">
<div class="text_cell_render border-box-sizing rendered_html">
<h2 id="Background">Background<a class="anchor-link" href="#Background">¶</a></h2><p><strong>Selection in evolutionary computation.</strong> Classical operators include random selection (no selective pressure), truncation (elite-based), tournament (pairwise or small-group competition), and <strong>lexicase</strong> selection, where individuals are filtered on objectives in a random order until a small set remains—favoring specialists on different objectives alongside generalists.</p>
<p><strong>Down-sampled lexicase</strong> applies lexicase-style filtering using only a random subset of objectives each event, lowering cost while retaining multi-objective structure.</p>
<p><strong>BarraCUDA / GPU-style analogy.</strong> Tournament and truncation map to reductions such as <strong>top-k</strong> or <strong>argmax</strong> over aggregate fitness. Lexicase requires <strong>per-objective comparisons</strong> and repeated filtering across the population—similar in spirit to <strong>batched scoring</strong> (e.g., one objective analogous to a matrix–like evaluation) combined with <strong>index selection and masking</strong>. Population maintenance corresponds to <strong>buffered genotypes and reusable index arrays</strong> each generation.</p>
</div>
</div>

<p><strong>Key findings.</strong> Structured selection pressures improve mean aggregate fitness relative to random baselines on this toy landscape. Lexicase maintains higher phenotype diversity than truncation while remaining competitive on fitness—consistent with the idea that lexicase-style filtering leaves room for objective-specific specialists. Mean Pareto-front counts illustrate how multi-objective structure can persist under lexicase relative to simpler aggregate-based schemes.</p>
<p><strong>ecoPrimals connection.</strong> <strong>Lexicase</strong> aligns with <strong>per-constraint primal evaluation</strong> (objectives as loosely coupled scoring dimensions). <strong>Multi-objective fitness</strong> maps naturally to multiple criteria per primal. <strong>Diversity maintenance</strong> resonates with ecological themes such as <strong>biomeOS species / niche management</strong>, where preserving variation is preferable to collapsing the population onto a single scalar optimum.</p>
